reason: The FAQ answer under 'What happens to my data when an Amazon EC2 instance terminates?' states both halves verbatim: instance store data persists only as long as the instance is alive, EBS data can persist independently of the instance life.

The quote is the second step of an example about a volume provisioned with 40,000 IOPS at 16KB; the claim drops that condition and states the 16,000 IOPS figure for any io2 Block Express volume at 256 KB, which the quote does not say (a volume provisioned with fewer IOPS would not reach it).
Verbatim match: when attached to EBS-optimized instances, io2 Block Express is designed to deliver within 10% of provisioned IOPS 99.9% of the time in a given year; condition and per-year scope kept.
The quote says io2 Block Express is designed for business-critical applications, offering 100X greater durability at 99.999% compared to other EBS volumes; the claim restates this exactly.

Under the io2 Block Express durability question the quote states that durability, snapshots and AZ replication protect against different failures and customers can use one, two, or all approaches; claim and displays match.
The two quotes give the workload description and the database examples (SAP HANA, Oracle, MS SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Cassandra) exactly as the claim lists them.

Under 'Can my application use Multi-Attach?' the quote lists the same three conditions (Windows Server Failover Cluster, NVMe reservations, application-level coordination) joined by 'or', as the claim does.
In the Multi-Attach section the quote says deleteOnTermination is determined by the last attached instance terminated and advises enabling or disabling it for all attached instances; claim matches.
Verbatim: EBS is a multi-tenant block storage service and employs rate limiting to avoid resource contention.
Verbatim: Provisioned IOPS SSD io2 Block Express and io1 volumes are available on all EC2 instance types.

The 16KB base I/O size is supported, but the quote states the dependence of the IOPS rate on I/O size only for io2 Block Express, and gives no 'so' causal link; the claim widens it to all Provisioned IOPS volumes and adds the causal link.
The answer 'Yes, you will be billed for the IOPS provisioned when it is disconnected from an instance' sits under the question about a Provisioned IOPS volume; claim and condition match.
The quote states the queue depth rule of one per 1000 provisioned IOPS in a minute for maximum consistency; the rounding condition is kept in the qualifiers.

The two quotes give the purpose (fully performant within a predictable amount of time) and the method (enter a desired initialization rate when launching from EBS-backed AMIs or creating volumes from snapshots).
Verbatim: at no additional charge, EBS volume data is replicated across multiple servers in an Availability Zone to prevent loss from the failure of any single component.
The quote says to set the Delete on termination flag to No for a root-partition EBS volume to persist outside the life of the instance; the claim and the root-volume condition match.
The quote says encrypted snapshots and AMIs using a customer-managed CMK can be shared with other AWS accounts; the claim states the same with the current name for the key.
The claim is scoped to what the FAQ lists, and the quote lists exactly these six volume types.
The two quotes give the detach, snapshot, reattach recommendation for attached volumes and the shut-down recommendation for root devices, as claimed.

The quotes say a 16 TB snapshot by design should take no longer than a 1 TB snapshot, and that actual time depends on factors including the data changed since the last snapshot; the 'by design' condition is kept.
Verbatim: each snapshot is given a unique identifier and customers can create volumes based on any of their existing snapshots.
The quote says snapshots protect against a volume failure and AZ replication protects against an AZ-level failure and provides faster recovery; claim matches.
Verbatim: snapshots only capture data written to the EBS volume, which might exclude data locally cached by the application or OS.
The answer 'No, snapshots are only available through the Amazon EC2 API' to the question about the regular Amazon S3 API supports both parts of the claim.
Verbatim: SSD-backed volumes are designed for transactional, IOPS-intensive database workloads, boot volumes, and workloads that require high IOPS.
Verbatim: st1 can drive throughput up to 500 MB/s, but performance is limited by the separate instance-level limit for EBS traffic; the maximum and the condition are kept.
The quote says st1 and sc1 performance scales linearly with volume size so there may not be as much benefit to stripe them; the hedged claim matches.
Verbatim: EBS Standard Volumes have been renamed to EBS Magnetic volumes.
Verbatim: striping multiple volumes can achieve up to 400,000 IOPS or 12,500 Mbps when attached to larger EC2 instances; unit and condition kept.
The quote recommends io2 Block Express for higher performance requirements without the operational management of striping; claim matches.
Under 'Does creating a copy of a volume affect the performance of the source volume?' the answer says the source volume performance is unaffected during or after the copy.
Verbatim: Volume Clones instantly create a copy of a volume within the same Availability Zone, with fast access to point-in-time data at single-digit millisecond latency.

The quote states the Free Tier includes 30 GB of storage, 2 million I/Os and 1 GB of snapshot storage with EBS; the July 15, 2025 condition for new customers is in the context and kept in the qualifiers.

The quote and context support up to 5 FSR snapshots per Region, including shared ones counted against your quota and not the owner's, but nothing in the evidence says the value is a default or adjustable (qualifiers default/adjustable true); the Service Quotas row in general-gr would support that if added as evidence.
Verbatim: billed for each minute FSR is enabled for a snapshot in a particular Availability Zone, pro-rated with a minimum of one hour.
Verbatim: one credit bucket per snapshot per Availability Zone, each volume created from an FSR-enabled snapshot consumes one credit; the less-than-one-credit condition is in the context.

For the 128 GiB example the second quote says a full bucket allows 8 initialized volumes simultaneously (8 credits), and the context shows the bucket-size formula giving 8 credits; claim and formula in the condition match the page.

The quotes give DSU-hour charging per snapshot and per AZ, per-minute billing with a one-hour minimum, and $0.75 per DSU-hour; the context names US-East (N. Virginia) as the example Region, as the claim states.
The quote states volumes up to 64,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s receive the full FSR benefit, and the context recommends initializing volumes above that; claim matches.
Verbatim: fast snapshot restore can be enabled on snapshots with a size of 16 TiB or less.
